title: Know your numbers
note: You cannot fix what you cannot see.

questions.q: Do you know your voluntary turnover for the last 12 months, by role?
questions.action: Pull 12 months of departures by role, so you know where turnover lives.

questions.q: Can you see turnover by manager, not just company-wide?
questions.action: Break turnover out by manager. In most companies a few teams account for most of the people who leave.

questions.q: Do you know what one departure really costs you, beyond recruiting fees?
questions.action: Price one departure across all 13 cost categories, not just job ads and agency fees.

questions.q: Do you track how many new hires leave in their first 90 days?
questions.action: Track first-90-day turnover on its own. It is usually the fastest number to move.

questions.q: Do you know which of your high performers are most likely to leave next?
questions.action: Score everyone for the next 90 days, so you know who needs a conversation before they resign.

questions.q: Do your leaders review retention numbers at least once a month?
questions.action: Put a short set of retention numbers in front of your leaders every month, with an owner for each.

title: Your managers
note: People leave managers more than they leave companies.

questions.q: Do managers have a regular one-on-one with every direct report?
questions.action: Set a standing one-on-one for every direct report, even 15 minutes every other week.

questions.q: Do managers hold Retention Talks with their best people before anyone resigns?
questions.action: Start Retention Talks with your highest performers this month: what keeps them, and what would make them leave.

questions.q: Are managers measured on the turnover of their own teams?
questions.action: Add 12-month team turnover to every manager's scorecard.

questions.q: Are new supervisors trained to coach, not just schedule and assign?
questions.action: Train new supervisors to coach in their first 90 days in the role.

questions.q: When someone resigns, does their manager's manager find out why?
questions.action: Have the skip-level manager talk to everyone who resigns, within a week.

questions.q: Do you act on what people who left told you, within 90 days?
questions.action: Pick the top reason people gave for leaving and fix one part of it within 90 days.

title: Hiring and the first 90 days
note: Many departures are decided at the door.

questions.q: Do you know what your longest-tenured top performers have in common?
questions.action: Find the traits your best long-tenured people share. That is your profile of who stays.

questions.q: Do you hire against that profile, not just a job description?
questions.action: Rewrite postings and interview questions around the profile of who stays and performs.

questions.q: Can you make an offer within 7 days of a strong interview?
questions.action: Cut your time to an offer to under 7 days. Good candidates take the first solid offer.

questions.q: Does every new hire have a named mentor for their first 90 days?
questions.action: Give every new hire a mentor from your best long-tenured people.

questions.q: Do new hires get a check-in at 30, 60 and 90 days?
questions.action: Schedule 30, 60 and 90-day check-ins for every new hire before their first day.

questions.q: Do you know which employers are hiring your people away, and what they offer?
questions.action: Find out who is hiring your people, what they offer, and where you already win.

title: Friction, pay and growth
note: The everyday reasons people start looking.

questions.q: Are schedules posted at least two weeks ahead, and kept?
questions.action: Post schedules two weeks ahead and hold them. Late changes push people out.

questions.q: Have you checked frontline pay against your local market in the last 12 months?
questions.action: Check frontline pay against the employers you compete with for people, role by role.

questions.q: Can people see a career path from their role to the next one, with timing?
questions.action: Publish a career path for your largest frontline role, with what it takes and when.

questions.q: Do you ask employees which fixes they want, and tell them what you did?
questions.action: Ask your people which fixes matter most, then close the loop and tell them what changed.

questions.q: Are overtime and the hardest shifts shared fairly?
questions.action: Share overtime and hard shifts by rotation, and cap mandatory overtime.

questions.q: Do the tools and systems people use every day work most of the time?
questions.action: Ask the front line which tool slows them down most, and fix that one first.
